classification.difficultyReason: Construct a triangle using two angles and a side, explain uniqueness using AAS, and reject impossible angle data.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Using a ruler and compasses only, construct a triangle $ABC$ in which $AB=12\text{ cm}$, $\angle A=45^\circ$ and $\angle B=60^\circ$. Measure the length of $AC$ to the nearest millimetre. Which congruence test tells you that your neighbour gets the same length?

answer.short:
$AC\approx10.8\text{ cm}$; AAS.

The two given angles and matching side determine congruent triangles.
answer.worked:
Draw $AB=12\text{ cm}$. At $A$, construct a perpendicular to $AB$ and bisect the right angle to obtain a $45^\circ$ ray. At $B$, construct a $60^\circ$ ray to $BA$ on the same side of $AB$, using an equilateral-triangle construction. Label the intersection of the rays $C$.

Measuring the constructed segment gives $AC\approx10.8\text{ cm}$ to the nearest millimetre.

Your neighbour's triangle has the same two angles and the matching side $AB$, so the triangles are congruent by AAS. Their matching sides $AC$ are therefore equal.

spec.description: Authored solution construction: a 12 cm base, a 45-degree ray at A, and a 60-degree ray at B intersect at C. Dashed auxiliary arcs illustrate angle constructions. Display size is schematic; students measure their own full-size construction.
spec.mathematics: A=(0,0), B=(12,0), C=(12sqrt(3)/(1+sqrt(3)),12sqrt(3)/(1+sqrt(3))). AC is approximately 10.8 cm.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Ajun claims to have constructed a triangle in which one side is $10\text{ cm}$ and the angles at each end of this side are $105^\circ$ and $80^\circ$. Comment on Ajun’s claim.

answer.worked:
$$105^\circ+80^\circ=185^\circ.$$

The two given angles already exceed the $180^\circ$ angle sum of a triangle. Ajun cannot have constructed such a triangle.
